Point-to-point delivery with a winch drop — the profile behind most medical and last-mile drone logistics: fly out, hover low over the delivery point to lower a package, fly home.

The drop hover is at 25 m, where winch delivery is actually done: low enough for a short cable, high enough to clear obstacles and keep rotor wash off people below. On a Trinity F90+ class aircraft it costs about 970 W against 116 W in cruise — more than EIGHT times the cruise power — because the aircraft is fully rotor-borne with no wing lift at all.

The vertical climbs are more expensive still, at about 1150-1180 W, since climbing adds the work of raising the aircraft on top of the cost of holding it up. Any profile that hovers and climbs mid-mission pays for it twice.

One thing this file cannot express: a real delivery aircraft is lighter going home by the mass of the package, and the model has no way to change weight mid-mission. The return legs are therefore pessimistic by a few percent.
